why: Standard reference works on the open commercial form of the gate-front town, and on the enclosed temple town as a distinct type, which is why our capital's monzen is drawn as open machi.<!-- A second kotobank page under the same headword is registered separately, because the two carry different entries. -->

It gives a castle town's temple count and where its temples were gathered. Its limits: Amagasaki was a castle town, larger than the setting's county town; the quarter was laid out in 1617 by the lord's order, gathering temples from the castle site, the older town, the surrounding district and the lord's own connections, so its 20 temples on the 1635 map are a planned concentration rather than what the town grew on its own, and they are the quarter's count, not every temple in the town; its placement at the northwest corner by the samurai houses is a Japanese castle-town device with no counterpart in a Chinese county seat; it hedges the purpose it gives ("it is also thought").

It gives a small castle town's temple count and where they stood. Its limits: a castle town, not a county seat. A temple quarter planned at the town's edge under a daimyo's patronage is a Japanese castle-town practice with no close counterpart in the Chinese county seat. The count is of the temples standing in the former town today, not a register from the period. It hedges the planning ("it is thought"). It gives no population, and no temple sizes or founding dates.

It gives an early-modern temple's main hall size, its halls' layout and the rule that temples of its rank keep a full set of halls. Its limits: a leading Sōtō Zen temple of the rank that had to hold the ninety-day monks' retreat, rebuilt and supported by the local lords, and standing in Shinshiro, a small lord's seat, not the countryside - larger than an ordinary parish temple; its halls about the forecourt are the Sōtō pattern, not every sect's; its meditation hall and monks' hall were kept for that retreat, and the page never says who lived in which hall; the buildings date from 1697 to 1893, and their tile roofs replace the main hall's first shingles and the two monks' halls' first thatch.
It gives the large end of a county seat's City God temple. Its limits: one exceptionally grand temple, not a typical one; it survives as a museum.
It states that block gates were the castle towns' night closure, not only Edo's, which is what lets this page say the monzen was barred like any block.

It says in general terms where a Japanese village's tutelary shrine stands - within the village or at its edge - and that the shrine ground is where the village gathers for its main observances. It gives no date or region, and names both sites without saying which was commoner or why a village chose one.
unsettled: The entry gives no date for the custom it summarizes, so the period of its evidence is not fixed by the table.

why: It is the one readable page giving the towpath's measurements, which size the hauling path on our river capital. Its limits are that its figures describe the preserved central stretch as it stands today, whose fabric is later than the Tang institution it dates.

unsettled: A fan wiki on a fictional game setting has no real period or region; the table cannot place it.
A fan wiki on a fictional game setting has no real period or region; the table cannot place it.

why: Two of its encyclopedias count the style among the sanctuaries designated National Treasures or Important Cultural Properties - more than half, more than 55 per cent. Both are Heibonsha's, so this is one publisher's count given twice, not two that confirm each other. The page does not say where the table behind the 55 per cent came from, or in what year its "at present" count was taken. The count is of designated buildings, which are the old and notable ones rather than a sample of village shrines; a further sentence on one-bay sanctuaries being the majority is about Kamakura-period survivals only, and is not used.

It defines the sacred tree as generally a tree in a shrine's precinct, roped with a shimenawa and revered, which is the tree the country-shrine sheet draws. It is a definition, not a count: it does not say how many shrines, or which ranks of shrine, kept one. It does not date the roped tree; its only historical example is the medieval Kasuga sacred tree. It speaks for Japan only. The shimenawa is a Japanese form, and the entry says nothing of China.
unsettled: The entry summarizes the custom as it is now and dates it only by a medieval example, so the period of its evidence is not fixed.

why: It gives the two measurements that bound the largest Japanese temple hall, standing and lost, which is how this page keeps its hall-size ceiling honest about which it means.

It says one sometimes sees small shrines in a precinct besides the main hall, and that the formal standard dividing the two classes of them was set at the high-ranking government shrines before the war. That standard belongs to the Meiji government's shrine ranking (1871-1945), which came after the Edo period this setting is modeled on, so the formal division is a modern rule; the page's only older anchor is Ise, whose classes it takes from the Engishiki shrine register (905) and the Enryaku ritual records (804). It does not say how often an ordinary or village shrine had one, nor how old the custom of small precinct shrines is.

It says the shogunate ordered the highways' difficult stretches (難所) paved with stone and names where that paving survives (Hakone and Kikugawa on the Tokaido; the 430 m at Kanaya is a 1991 reconstruction), which says which kind of stretch was stone but gives no length or share of a Japanese road. It also names stone on temple approaches, on some city streets, on the Ryukyu kingdom's official roads and at Kuragari pass (laid by the Koriyama domain, not the shogunate), so it does not carry that stone was found only on the highways' difficult stretches. Its general account of the bare-earth road is not about Japan in particular (its examples are European). The article carries a banner saying it lacks sources, and the shogunate's order is itself uncited: its footnotes are tourist-association pages on the surviving stretches. It says nothing of Japanese village lanes.

Its footnotes lead mostly to Takebe Ken'ichi's 2015 road history 道路の日本史 and to Asai Kenji's popular road dictionaries. The late-Edo register of the highways' post towns and villages (宿村大概帳) reaches it only through those books, so a figure is carried from it only where it rests on Takebe. It describes the dressing of sand and gravel, the stone-paved exceptions and the villages' assigned stretches of upkeep. It describes the shogunate's trunk roads, the best-kept in the country, not village lanes or a domain's lesser roads. Its only specific sand dressing (Asakusa sand mixed with sea sand, the road built higher in the middle) is a 1648 order for Edo's city streets, not for the highways.

It places ropes, figures and sandals of straw at the village boundary across rural Japan and names the districts around Kinki where the rope is concentrated, which is what makes it a regional form rather than a universal one. Its list of districts around Kinki rests on the distribution map in Inami Toshihide's 1993 study of boundary charms, which it cites and which is the work that carries that claim, and its account of the rope's origin is one theory among several, taken from a museum lecture. It describes the custom as it survives today and as twentieth-century folklorists recorded it; its only evidence of age is medieval picture scrolls showing a rope hung round a single house in ritual abstinence, not across a village's boundary, and it gives no count of villages and no date for how old any one rope is.

It gives the form of the mounds - banks either side of the road, fenced on top - and the measurements of one of them, from a period plan. The measurements are of a single post town's mound (the bank is about 2.5 m high, and its fence adds another 75 cm), and a second period illustration of that same mound, in the Kanagawa sunago, draws it as a square mound like a milestone mound instead, so even its form is not settled. It hedges on how much the mounds still mattered late in the period; it describes post towns on the main highway only.

It lists two scholarly works (Nishigaki in the Nihonshi daijiten, 1994; Matsubara's "Bōji-kō", 2006) but ties no sentence to them, so it is used for the shape of the practice and not for any figure. It says what boundary markers were made of - posts of wood or stone, sometimes a rock or a standing tree - and gives no size, height or spacing. Its scope is ancient and medieval precincts and estates, not the Edo village, so it shows the practice's age and materials rather than how an Edo village's line was marked.

It sets out the two forms a village takes along a road - houses on both sides with little trade, or packed close with shops and lodging - and says they look alike in plan. The categories are those of modern settlement geography, borrowed from German usage, not Edo terms, and the article gives no share of villages in either form. Its road- and street-village examples are Japanese only (road villages common in Edo-period new-field settlements such as Santome Shinden; street villages such as market towns, post towns and temple-gate towns, many of which later grew into regional cities). It names no road or street village in China; its one mention of China is the Yangtze delta, as an example of the marsh village. Of the other forms, only two bear on us. The clustered village it calls widespread across Japan and most common in Kinki and Hokuriku. For the marsh village it gives Japanese examples (the ring-levee villages of the lower Kiso rivers, the lower Tone water country). The green village and the round village it places in Europe only.

It says where rest stops were set, what stood there and who set them up. Its remark that a rest stop grown into an in-between station had inns is loose: it notes only that the shogunate strictly limited such places, while the article on the in-between station says lodging there was forbidden in principle and allowed only when the post towns overflowed.

It says where Edo ferries ran - where a bridge was hard to build or not permitted - in a sentence it gives no citation for, and records a shogunate-designated ferry run by farmers (the Yagiri ferry) on the word of two tourist-board pages. Its Edo section is short; its boat figures for the Banyu ferry say "up to 20" where the ministry page it cites says "about 20", and most of the article is about modern ferries.

It lays out two real ferry landings - the river office, the notice board, the boatmen's huts, the boats with their kinds, numbers and sizes, the crews, and who held the contract - the nearest thing found to a description of a landing, though it lists what stood there without saying where each thing stood or how large it was, so it is not a plan. It gives the ban on bridging the great rivers only as competing theories (a river as a checkpoint, protecting the post towns and river porters, weak bridge-building), not a settled reason. Both are ferries on the busiest highway under shogunate regulation, far larger than a crossing a village would keep for itself.

It attests the ford as a regulated crossing where no bridge was built, and the depth at which it closed. Its own references are the Shimada city and Shimada tourism association pages, a dictionary entry (Kotobank) and a National Diet Library reference answer, so it carries the shape of the system, and its closing depth only as far as those pages carry it. Its details are drawn from the Oi river crossing at Shimada, the best-documented and largest, a crossing the shogunate regulated on a main highway, and may not hold for a smaller ford.

It gives the one clear case of a ruling family's mortuary precinct standing on a wooded rise across the river from the castle, the form our capital's lineage precinct may take. The Date were one of the greatest houses in the country, so the precinct is an upper case, and the buildings that stand are reconstructions after the fire of 1945, which leaves the siting untouched.

It gives the geographer's name for a settlement that grows as a strip along a highway because it lives by the traffic, which is the form a town's edge takes when houses run out along the road. It gives no lengths, no dates and no example, and it defines a settlement form rather than saying how any one town ended.
unsettled: The entries are modern geographers' definitions with no date, so the period of their evidence is not fixed.

why: It is the plainest readable statement that a Japanese city's built ground ran on out along its highways past the planned core, and that the government later caught up with it by taking the new strips into the town. Its limits: Edo was the largest city in the country, a capital rather than a town, so its highway strips are an upper case; and the dating is hedged in places ("around the Kan'ei era").

It says what the wood nearest a settlement was made of and what it was for, in a forest scientist's words, which is what the wood drawn at a town's margin needs. Its only dates are the dictionary's two example quotations of the word, from 1903 and 1915, both after the Meiji Restoration, so it does not show the woods or the word before then; it hedges with "often"; and it gives no size of such a wood or distance from the settlement, so it supports what the wood was and what grew in it, not how much of it to draw; and its note that such woods are valuable near cities is about their conservation value today, not their use in the past.
unsettled: The definition is modern with examples only from 1903 and 1915, while the record applies it to the premodern wood.

why: It gives, from the national forestry authority, both what the near woods were for and what they looked like - thin, low, many-stemmed trees regrowing from the stump - which is the look of a worked wood at a settlement's edge. Its history is a sentence, undated beyond "before Meiji", and it describes Japan in general rather than any town's margin. The page dates only the uses to before Meiji; the twenty-to-thirty-year cycle and the thin, low look are left undated and are those of the charcoal woods managed into the twentieth century. Forest historians find that many hills near Edo-period settlements, in the crowded regions, had been cut down to grass, pine scrub or bare slopes by early Meiji. So a well-kept coppice at a town's edge is one likely state of the near woods, not the only one.

It states that the court's weaving was confined to three cities, which is why our capital gets a purveyor and not an imperial works. It gives no headcount, and the arrangement is the QING court's, so the negative drawn from it - no imperial works at a provincial seat - is one dynasty's organization of court supply carried across the period.

It states the general arrangement of temple and school in one sentence. That sentence carries no footnote of its own (the article's reading list names Gao Mingshi's paper on the Sui-Tang temple-school system, which this project has not read), so it is used for the shape of the arrangement and not as an authority. The counts and site areas it gives elsewhere (temples across China, courtyards per temple, a few surviving temples' areas) describe surviving and often rebuilt temples, and are not used. It describes China: it says Korean temples put the school in front and the temple behind, and its Japan section is only a list of temples, so it gives no Japanese pattern.

It is a county-tier Confucian temple with a measured main hall and a stated place inside the wall. Its hall figures come from the temple's own former website, not a survey. The site inside the west gate is a relocation after the 1853-55 fighting and a fire on the old site, onto a vacant government plot; for five and a half centuries before, the temple stood east of the county yamen, so the present site is no guide to where a county put its temple. The building measured is a late-Qing rebuilding, restored in 1979 and 1997-99, and one county's temple is one example.

It gives a prefectural school-temple's full set of buildings and one measured hall (five bays by three, 374 square metres of floor inside, 16.4 metres high). Both the list and the measurements rest on the paper it cites, Bi Xiaofang and Cheng Jianjun's analysis of the hall in Southern Architecture (南方建筑), 2015. Only the hall survives, so the list is of what the complex held at some undated time before the exams ended in 1905, not a plan with sizes. The hall is the rebuilding after the 1602 fire, repaired four times under the Qing and used as an auditorium and a dance hall after 1949. It is a far-southern (Guangdong) building whose frame mixes the southern pierced-post system with the beam-lifting one, so its construction is regional, and a county's school-temple would be smaller.

It is a famous provincial academy that survives, and the article gives its site area. Its 21,000 square metres has no footnote of its own (the paragraph's one reference is a 2007 web page on the academy's buildings), and it does not say what the figure takes in - the Ming axis ran on past the compound to the Xiang River and the mountain top. It is one of the four great academies of China, made Hunan's provincial academy by an edict of 1733, and the article calls it the largest surviving academy in China, so it bounds an academy's size from above rather than showing a typical one. Its layout is Ming and Qing, but much of what stands was rebuilt: after Japanese bombing in 1938 and 1941 and near-ruin in the Cultural Revolution it reopened in 1986 after five years' repair, the Chongsheng shrine and Minglun hall were rebuilt in 2003-04, and the dormitory ranges date from 1903, when it became a modern school. And the article places the academy's Confucian temple on the axis in one passage and to one side of it in another.

It names the Zen seven halls in English and says the conventions vary by school and era. Its covered corridors are said of Eiheiji, a great mountain head temple, not of Zen temples in general, still less of a town temple. It gives no date for any hall or corridor, and Eiheiji's oldest standing building is the gate rebuilt in 1749. So it shows the layout and names of the halls, and cannot show that the medieval temple had these corridors.
